p:
Well, we had to establish, you know, it's a little bit, it's a little bit technical, but when we would do the, uh, the canvassing that used to occur all after Election Day, uh, and we really did think, uh, when the state legislature passed that, that that was going to be highly problematic for us if we had to do it ahead of time. What we found out was, with appropriate planning and appropriate, appropriate readjustment of full-time staff, we didn't have as many problems as we thought we were going to have. And in fact, um, it has turned out to be a blessing not only for the Board of Elections but for, uh, the elected officials and, and the voters as well, because we have to stop canvassing mail ballots on the Friday before the Tuesday, uh, uh, of Election Day.

What that means is the overwhelming majority of mail ballots, which we're calling them now instead of absentee ballots, are canvassed and completed before Election Day. Now we can't publish the results um, until 9 o'clock on Election Day. But now when you're looking at election results, you're seeing all of the results from Election Day, all of the results from early voting, and the overwhelming majority of mail ballots. So all of that back-end rancor that used to happen— how come the Board of Elections can't, you know, count all the ballots and why is it taking so long? Doesn't happen anymore.

Yeah, we should, we should point out we're the fastest also in the state. I'm going to keep being a cheerleader for the New York City Board of Elections. The fastest returns in the entire New York state is the New York City Board of Elections by roughly 9:30-ish, and you have over 80, 90% in. And that's because of effective work by great people. There are people watching right now, I'm sure, at their desk at the board, and, you know, we want to thank them.

When it was 100-degree weather during the primary February, people showed up and, and were, and were there. When it was a blizzard, people showed up. So these are our neighbors. They're not, you know, they don't come from Mars. They're our poll workers, our staff members do an excellent job and continue to and I just wanted the one message I want them to hear Mike and I say is that we honor them for their service.

And Councilman, uh, I know you want to get on to the, the next thing, but I also want to extend another thank you to the City Council. Uh, because when we made that presentation, I think it was back in 2019, 2018, whatever it was, uh, we made the presentation to the City Council that we needed, um, we needed laptops, uh, for the poll sites so that we could upload the results from the poll sites. That was an investment that continues to pay dividends today because that's one of the major things that allows us to get our results, uh, so quickly on election night.

Let me take advantage, if I may, Madam Chair, of the fact that we're all Staten Islanders. You know, we heard a lot during the recent

snowstorm when the Mayor was explaining the difficulties of plowing Staten Island about the unique topography of Staten Island and the unique difficulty of catering to a borough like that. Are there any operational challenges unique to boroughs like Staten Island, whether it's related to geography, site availability, staffing, that the board has had to address in recent election cycles?

Well, let's stick with Staten Island just for, just for a second, and we'll get to, uh, other areas in the city. Uh, one of the problems that Staten Island has is because of its, uh, unique character, not necessarily topography. We don't have, uh, the plethora of government-owned buildings, say, that some other boroughs might have in a concentration. Uh, so we have what we call in, in inside the board as deserts within Staten Island where we don't have real options. We only have one option. This is the place, it's the only place that's available, it's the place we have to use. So when you hear some complaints about some locations in Staten Island— we won't name them— that's one of the reasons. In terms of topography,

uh, one of the most difficult places in terms of topography is Washington Heights. Uh, we had, we had moved, we had moved a poll site literally one block in Washington Heights, and we got— this was a number of years ago— and got a crazy number of complaints.
I remember.

You know, and we went to the place to visit it, and we brought one of the experts with us, and he said to me, uh, a term that I had never heard before. He, he called it a hand burner, meaning that the block was so steep that if somebody was a manual wheelchair user, they would not be able to stop the wheelchair with their bare hands. And that was not a— that was not a term of art, it was a term within that accessibility, uh, uh, evaluation. So of course, you, you know, challenges occur when you— we learned a lesson from that. You can't look at a map, a flat piece of paper, and necessarily come to the best conclusion. You really have to evaluate, uh, these, uh, these matters specific to, uh, the locations that you're dealing with.

And that's why we dovetail to Council Member, Council Members, Chairs. If you

have issues with regards to an early voting location, please let us know because we know you are the experts in your districts. So please evaluate, send us, uh, send us sites you want us to survey and look into. They won't always work, and they won't— sometimes they don't even want you there or us there. So, but we're happy to work with any and all who, who want us to look at different sites.

And one of the one of the things that led to the expansion, A, the establishment of, and then B, the expansion of the number of ramp vendors that we use was an acknowledgement that temporarily retrofitting a location is often the better alternative than moving the poll site somewhere else. And that was an evaluation that we made. We get much, much less complaints about poll sites and poll site relocations, although they still do happen, but not nearly with the frequency that they used to happen years ago.

Lastly, Madam Chair, I think between the 4 of us— the 2 of you and the 2 of us— we've collectively run in 21 elections, most of those the Chair. But, um, the point is - The point

is, uh, you guys know your way around, uh, the, the, that aspect of the electoral arena as well. And you know how much skepticism there is among the public about election integrity and voter integrity. In, uh, 2004 when President Bush won, you had a lot of Democrats claiming that the machines in Ohio were rigged, or some version of the the, uh, er, the result was inaccurate. In 2020, when President Biden won, you had a lot of Republicans voicing similar skepticism. So with that, public confidence in elections is pretty critical to democracy. Can, can you walk us through the safeguards that the New York City Board of Elections has in place to ensure that the ballots are secure, voter rolls are accurate, and that every vote cast in New York City is counted properly?

So New York state election law has probably one of the most stringent, uh, bodies of law in the country with respect to maintaining ballot integrity. Now, one of the things that they, that they did from the very beginning— and I, and it was, uh, a matter of robust debate uh, in the State Board of Elections and in the state legislature was they do

not allow voting machines at poll sites to be networked. There is the potential to have an air card within those voting machines that would allow the, uh, results to be, uh, trans— uh, transmitted that way. And there's also the potential of the voting machines being linked from one to the other. None of that is permitted, uh, in New York State. So when you, when you vote on a particular voting machine, the ballot goes in, it gets kept, uh, into the, uh, into a secure box, uh, in that cabinet that you're voting on. But more importantly than all of that, there's no way to externally access that machine to be able to change the vote, the, the vote totals. You would have to have access, physical access to, to that voting machine, which would mean if you were gonna change vote totals for any, in any great way, people would have to go into the 1,200 poll sites on Election Day, somehow remain invisible and undetected, and then be able to physically access, uh, the, uh, the, the, the ports on the back of the machine to change the vote totals, and then somehow change those vote totals on the paper too, so that if

we— when we detected that there was a problem, the recount of the paper would match, uh, the, uh, electronic totals. It is a, it is a virtual, uh, extreme impossibility.

And it's also with use of the— with our partner agencies, the NYPD, which doesn't happen everywhere, um, a chain of custody of ballots with the NYPD as well. And it's, you know, it's important to note that when we do either sense or believe that there is a— any type of, uh, election interference, we have made several referrals to both the federal, uh, city and state agencies for prosecution.

And we, and we see that typically, you know, with, uh, uh, either the absentee process or the voter registration process, not with the Election Day process. And then post-election, which I neglected to mention, uh, there is an audit process that is required by state election law. You'll hear it called a 3% audit, but it's really not. It, it could be up to 100% audit but it's 3%. If there's a problem with the 3%, it goes to an additional 5%, which would be 8, and then up the chain.

In my 13 years, there's only been one time where it's— where any audit has gone beyond 3%, and it was in a few districts, uh, in the Bronx about 8 or 9 years ago. Uh, so we're confident, uh, in the integrity of the system and we're further confident with the integrity of our employees, uh, who are responsible, uh, for making sure that all of these vote totals are calculated properly.

Thank you both and next time you're here, I hope you'll bring the, the board's operations manager, Georgia Katsamanis, with you so we could thank her on behalf of the public for the great work she's doing as well.
Well, she's watching it, uh, from her desk.
And probably cursing you right now.
So you just thanked her. So, uh, thank you.

Thank you very much. So, um, justice involves voters. There are many individuals in our jail system that are eligible to vote as they are either awaiting trial and haven't been convicted of a crime or have only been convicted of a

misdemeanor. According to the Fiscal '25 MMR data, the city's jail population has grown each year since '21. It is quite possible that there are also many who are eligible to vote that are either unaware or have trouble figuring out how to vote. And I know League of Women Voters, Legal Aid, and so on, they're all trying to make this barrier less so that people can vote. So what are the barriers to facilitate voting? How is voter eligibility communicated to those in the facility at Rikers in particular? What lessons have you learned from election cycles? I know there has been some effort to make this a reality for people. What coordination exists between the board and agencies such as probation and correction? And how are you addressing misinformation in justice-involved communities where individuals may incorrectly believe they are permanently barred from voting? I hear a lot when I go to NYCHA Family Days that people feel this is not you, this is just the way our society works, that they have completed everything in terms of their sentence, but they do not feel they can vote. That's a real problem.

Well, just the umbrella, and then, and then I guess Mike will— he, he's very well schooled on this, having served as a probation officer and, uh, as the board Chair. But we have instituted a working group with all interested parties that speaks every single month, and they've done a great job of working to, uh, working with both the interest groups and the Department of Corrections, uh, to ensure that they, they have a system in place that any incarcerated individuals can, can vote. Uh, I don't know, Mike, if you—

Right, so it is the, um, responsibility of the New York City Department of Corrections to impart, uh, the information to those uh, whose care they are responsible for, for the period that they remain incarcerated. Um, so in the past, it was the board doing its job and the Department of, uh, Corrections, uh, doing its job and I don't want to say never the twain shall meet, but they were further apart than they should have been. And since, uh, Council Member Morano already mentioned, uh, Ms Katsamanis, I'll mention her again. Uh, our operations manager really took, uh, the bull

by, uh, the horns and, uh, insinuated the board into the process more than we had been in the past. And one of the things, uh, that we did, uh, which I think has really helped the Department of Corrections, um, is we have now an internal process where all of the documentation that needs to to be turned over to the Department of Corrections with respect to, uh, voting-eligible, uh, incarcerated individuals are now transmitted internally to the Queens office, uh, and it's kind of a one-stop shopping for the Department of Corrections. Uh, they get all the information that they, they need, and all of the exchange of documents is handled out of the Queens office, uh, so that we can main— better maintain, um, control over it. But also, uh, this— the Department of Corrections doesn't have a tremendous amount of staff that's, uh, dedicated to this process, and they used to go from borough office to borough office. So instead of them circling all around the city, we work with them, uh, we, uh justify the numbers every month to make sure that we're not missing anything or nothing's, uh, falling through the cracks. Um, and from what I understand has, has been

reported to me, uh, although I'm not as maybe well-versed— I'm certainly not as well-versed in it as Ms. Katsamanis— but that the Legal Aid Society, who works closely, uh, in this process, has been largely, uh, complementary, uh, of the board's efforts and our assistance to, uh, the Department of Corrections in, in making this process work better.

No, I think it's improving. I know that there are many, I don't know, something like almost maybe 500 people, but there were thousands registered. So it's a hard, I'm not gonna say it's easy, but is there a portion of the budget that is allocated toward this effort in terms of marketing, in terms of staffing, or is it just—

Well, so we don't have direct, we don't have direct access to the individuals that are incarcerated. But we provide the Department of Corrections all of the information, uh, that they need and as it's updated, as its updates are required, we, we update.

And I don't believe it's a budgetary issue. We could— so we could supply them with whatever they need. They have, uh, they have sufficient budget as well. I think this is— some

people don't engage as well. Like, just because you're registered and you— it doesn't mean you wanna partake in the system any more than anybody in Staten Island or Manhattan or whatever does. So, um, but we're, we're committed to working and continue on a monthly basis. If people can build a better mousetrap, we're, we're happy to be a partner in that to the extent we can.

So a couple things in terms of the budget as well, uh, we have over 5 million registered voters in the city of New York when you, when you add inactive and, and active voters. So if we're talking about, you know, 500 to 1,000 individuals from the Department of Corrections, it really is a drop in the bucket in terms of, uh, our voter processing, uh, budget. So that's— it's not going to be a funding issue. One of the challenges, I think, in fairness to the Department of Corrections, uh, is that they're dealing with a transient population, and they might touch, uh, an individual, uh, with respect to voting uh, information and then that individual either makes bail or has their case resolved and gets out, or has

their case resolved and moves on to the State Department, uh, of, uh, Division of Corrections. So, you know-
Or the ballot expires.

Yeah and it's a, it's a little bit of a moving target for them as well, uh, but we certainly, uh, want to be, uh, and, and should be and want to be as helpful in that process as we can because our job is to, is to service all of the voters of the city of New York, or eligible voters of the City of New York.

Okay, so what hap— just once you say, for instance, you do get, um, registered, you're there for a series— and the League of Women Voters is there often, and so is Legal Aid. They're both trying. And so once you are registered, I guess there's some, you know, it's a pretty major election coming up in November and there's some primaries. So if you're there, then the ballot would go— would be filled out there and then brought back to Queens. Is that the idea? Is that how you would— how you would—

Right and before, I think the big change was there was no tracking in place for— that I

would say unified tracking between the, the— between the Department of Corrections and the board over how many are dropped off and how many are processed back. It used to be that the Department of Corrections would drop off what they dropped off, we'd process what we processed, and nobody was comparing numbers. That's now happening on a monthly basis to make sure that we, uh, prevent as many as we possibly and humanly can, uh, from falling through the cracks.
Okay, you wanna say—

I was just gonna— it's not an ignored population, it's one that we're working on. And quite frankly, the, the benefit of having tracking throughout, uh, has been a benefit to everybody in the city because we're able to see where your ballot is, where it is along the process, when it's mailed and, and, uh, working with the post office, we can see what's coming back. So it's been a— it, it's been a good endeavor to have that tracking system throughout.
Okay.

And also, we compare numbers like you should, kind of like little mini audits every month with the Department of Corrections and, and the

Board of Elections and then we're on the same page when those numbers are shared with the Legal Aid Society. So we think that that's also contributing to more faith in the system on the part of the Legal Aid Society because they're not getting one set of numbers from the Department of Corrections and an apparently different set of numbers from the board.

Okay, so the tracking is working. Um, regarding voter privacy, uh, related to Local Law 31 of '25, voter privacy and awareness obviously are necessary. You know that as well as I do. How many voters currently utilize confidential voter registration status under, uh, election law 5-110, and what is the average processing time for these requests?
It's about 150, I would say, city, uh, citywide.
150, okay.
Um, yeah, and it's within 24 to 48 hours it's processed. We had a scenario that existed not too long ago where it was processed within 8 hours.
Okay.
We recognize the delicate nature of the request and how sometimes the impact on it is immediate, uh, so we, we do not take a back seat to something so serious.
So how do you tell voters about this available protection? You know, obviously I passed a bill recently for the domestic violence, uh—

Yeah, that's right. So the CFPB was charged— the CFPB was charged with that through, uh, um, through your bill. However, we have it on our website, it's on the state board's website, um, it's available for people. We have— I believe we have a flyer on it as well, but, um, but we encourage people to, you know, should they require or need that protection, to avail themselves of it, because we will process it right away. It's a very serious, very significant issue that we are, uh, um, happy to ensure that proper adjudication of.

And the state law was amended, uh, when it first, uh, was, uh, initiated, an individual who was the victim of domestic violence had to actually go to court and file. So the good thing is now there's a State Board of Elections, uh,

promulgated form that allows the, the, the victim of domestic violence, uh, to simply fill out the form, uh, and then we, uh, we process it, uh, and it's, it's much easier for, uh, for those individuals that need it.

Okay, and do you have any way of sort of knowing whether or not these campaigns that do say you can be private in your vote are reaching the residents and people who need it? Do you have any way of doing that?
I mean, it's hard for us to tell because how do you define, uh, the domestic violence population?
Or any— I mean, there are other populations too. It's not just

Well, even with the, even with the judges, I mean, um, we, we have, uh, worked closely, uh, with, with the federal court, uh, most recently, but before that, the state courts. Um, the, the alternative for a judge that wants their, uh, address to become private is that they have to vote, uh, either, uh, by affidavit or in the office. And what we've seen so far is, um, there hasn't been a mass migration towards that process. There have been

some, uh, but, you know, a lot of people still like to vote on the machine.
No, I agree. They just may not know about it though. I'm just, you know, listen-
Well, there has been internal, uh, education processes in place in both the state, uh, Office of Court Administration, uh, and at least one district of the federal court that we've dealt with.

And my understanding is the nonprofits in that sector, and primarily, uh, DV, are very well aware and have advised them to do that as a way of taking their names off a list that, uh, the potential, uh, somebody can see.
Okay. This is a Civics for All week in the City Department of Education. So 16 and 17-year-olds can pre-register to vote, as you know.
My daughter did.

I make sure that they do. So what steps are you taking to ensure you receive voter information or registration so that they can vote when they're 18? What data do you do? Because you're tracking, I hope, what is, uh, signed up for, um, and are there some, uh, school district disparities? Um,

how do you evaluate the success of this voter registration in high schools? Uh, do you participate in Civics for All? Or— I was there this morning and yesterday at the programs and if legislation lowering the age— this is my issue, I know you don't like it— the voting age for municipal elections were enacted, what changes would be required and what timeline? I think that has to be done by the state and not the city. I tried this.
So, uh, my question is really how do we get the 16 and 17-year-olds in the high schools to pre-register and how are you tracking it?

So we cooperate, uh, with the Department of - of education. When, when this was first brought up, I could tell you, uh, when there was an expansion of Local Law 29, uh, and an Executive Order that was related to that, uh, it was Executive Order Number 1 in the de Blasio Administration. Um, the board, uh, quite frankly, uh, resisted being, uh, the police for city agencies and our position at the time uh, and remains so, uh, to some extent, is that this— to the extent that those agencies, whether it be the Department of Education or others, have a reporting, uh, requirement to the

City Council, then it's their responsibility, uh, as, uh, you're kind of co-equal, uh, partners in government to make sure that they're reporting accurately. It's not not really— the board should not be put in the middle as a, a go-between or, or a policing of the city agencies. That having been said, um, we understand that there's been certain requirements imposed upon the Department of Education by the City Charter, and they have asked us, uh, to issue voter registration forms with a code on them. So you may recall that Code D is, uh, for the CUNY. We're now gonna do a code S, which is starting with the printing of the new voter registration forms for this year, a code S for the schools, uh, so that they can, uh, more accurately, uh, track, uh, the process, uh, from their end, the processed, um, voter registration forms. From our end, those forms come in like every other form, and we process them the same way that we process all of the other voter registration forms. With respect to the ages, uh, 16s and 17-year-olds, um, it is built into the system that those individuals get put into the system as future voters,

and when their birth date hits, the system automatically, uh, graduates them, uh, for lack of a better term, into a full voter.
And I could tell you it works because my daughter did. So, um, and so it works well. We, we did participate in, uh, Civic Week this week. We did have the code— I was— it 8 or S?
S.

S, Okay, we did have it active, and there was, uh, City Council legislation on this as well, uh, that was passed last year. So we, we work fully with our friends at the Department of Ed, and, um, and, you know, do visit upon being— upon request as well.

Okay, I mean, with all do respect for DOE, they have lots of, uh, issues to address. And I just wanna make sure that this is one of them. So I think it has to be all hands on deck in order to get these young people registered. I mean, you have a receptive audience. If they register at this early age, and then they're automatically registered to vote, that's huge.
Yeah, my daughter did it when she got her, uh, when she got her, uh, driver's permit.
Learner's permit. Yeah, yeah but that's your daughter.
Yes. Well, I'm just—

Not everybody else, I'm just saying. So I'm just, you know, having known thousands and thousands of high school students, it would be fabulous to get them registered and this is one way to do it. So I'm just saying, I think we should put more effort into it. I understand DOE is supposed to be doing that. They're supposed to be doing the outreach but I think also you, you, you all should be doing the same thing.

The, the other thing though, that I, that I think we have to give some thought on, uh, and I'm, and I, recognize that this is not a, a fully and complete thought to a resolution and, uh, of the problem. Um, you hand a kid today a pen and a piece of paper, they look at you like you're crazy. We have to migrate this process to the, uh, online voter registration process.
What are you doing about that?

Uh, well, the Department of Education asks us for like 100,000 pieces of paper. Um, one of the, one of the feedbacks that we've gotten from not only the Department of Education but other entities that do online, that do voter registration drives, is there is no process in place for them to track if it goes into the, uh, electronic system, and that the paper allows, uh, more accurate tracking. But if the paper is allowing for more accurate tracking but not accommodating a population that is otherwise resistant to filling out pieces of paper, you know, I think that's a conversation worth having. That's like a software issue. Why is— why can't this be addressed?

We have overcome it. That's with, with the, with the new codes that we have employed. Well, we can, but now it's about having our, our friends and colleagues in, in schools adopt the model of bringing more iPads or laptops in order to register and not hard copy. But, you know, it's a work in progress. We're doing well. We just have to -
So, you can't track the S if it's online. Who would fix that? Is that a— who, who—

No, what I'm saying the opposite. I'm saying the opposite. What I'm saying is that the entities that are doing the voter registration drives can't track how many individuals they processed if it's online.
Well, why not? That's what I'm saying. In other words, you're in the— you— what— you could track it if they use your code, right?
Right, it's a hurdle that we've overcome just this year.
You can track it.
Yeah.
But so you'd have to take some paper and some online and combine them, right, for the tracking.

Yeah, we, we can convey to the Department of Ed, should they want, what, what and whom, how much registrations we've had this year alone or next year. That's, that's the ultimate goal of it, which, which we've—
It's just about— I don't think it's an impossible task. What it is, is it's about breaking an old habit.
Yeah.

People are used to doing it this way and used to handing out the forms. And, you know, we need to get to the point where the, the younger folks, especially whether it's school students or, you know, millennials as they say, have to know that they can pick up their cell phone and do it right from their cell phone.

I'm aware of that, but I'm just— well, it's not going to be cell phone in the high schools, Mike, in case you didn't know, but it could be, uh, laptop. So I think we should work— we'll work with DOE to try to get them to do it but as long— you can count. Somebody may still do it on paper. We put the two together, you gotta—
Right.
It's not hard.
Correct.

One plus the other is what the total is. All right, so that's something to work on for us. Um, homeless people who are housing

instability situations. Obviously it's hard for them to receive voter information. Voter registration forms ask for an address. I think you can vote without having a permanent address, but please answer that. What steps have you taken to deal and get people who are homeless to understand that they can vote? And, um, what guidance is provided to poll workers when somebody comes in, when they do list a shelter or is it park bench? I've seen that. Um, do you coordinate with the outreach, uh, workers at different shelters? Have you conducted outreach to city shelters or to supportive housing facilities? And again, do you have data? That's another place where you collect data on this issue.

Yeah, so the education part of that is the, uh, we work with, uh, the Campaign Finance Board because that falls into, uh, their responsibility, and we provide them, uh, with updated information to make sure that, you know, uh, that Madam Chair may remember a few years back when there was some misinformation that was promulgated with respect to, uh, who was eligible to vote if they were, uh, a convicted felon. And we worked with the Campaign Finance Board to make sure that they had uh,

the correct and updated information to avoid that from happening again in the future. Um, and in, in similar regard, when there are, um, outreach requirements that the, the, the Campaign Finance Board has, we, uh, have worked, uh, very closely with them to make sure that they have the accurate information. In terms of, uh, special, uh, instructions to the poll poll workers. The system, the registration system, is designed to accommodate, uh, people who don't have a permanent address, and it's in the system. So as long as— if the person shows up to vote, uh, there's nothing that really needs to be done on the part of the poll worker. They show up to vote, they give them their— if their name, it comes up on, on the iPad, uh, they sign their signature uh, and move on.
Right and, but in terms of there's no tracking for those who are in shelters or in, I would just call temporary housing, there's no tracking for that?
There's not.

No and, and again, similar to the incarcerated population, that is also a very transient population within the City of New York. Uh, so I, I honestly can't see how we could implement an effective tracking system, uh, that involves individuals who may be, uh, on the move on a regular basis.

Alright, I thank you very much. I would look forward to dealing with that one school that is quite upset and trying to find another location. We can work with you on that if you want, and then, um, you know, we work with you on your capital needs that are more immediate with your vans, and then just look forward to, um, getting as many people as possible to vote. I think obviously in the last election many more people did vote but what was the new number that you had in terms of voting for last election?
Uh, it was north of 2 million.
North of 2 million, okay, alright.
I don't know the exact number, right, which is, uh, that was in the mail.

I do have one more question. Thank you for reminding me. Council Member Dinowitz has a question. He's - I forgot that he's, uh, had a question. Let me read to you right now. Hold on, hold on. Yeah, I know. I'm just trying to find it. Here it is. Okay. It is. Thank you for reminding me. I think he sent a letter to you in 2024 outlining the concerns about the way party positions appear on primary election ballots, and he didn't get a response. So number 1, party positions such as District leader, state Committee appear on the primary ballot when there's a contested primary. How -historically there were two seats for each position within an assembly district, one designed for a male and one designed for a female, and the ballots reflected that structure.
